strengths: The paper provides the first parameterized-complexity analysis of the Satisfiability problem for Pearl's Causal Hierarchy, opening a genuinely new research direction on top of an established and well-motivated classical NP/∃R-hardness landscape.

The technical contribution is non-trivial and interesting: the authors depart from the standard dynamic-programming approach typically used for treewidth-based algorithms (which they convincingly argue is fundamentally incompatible with the SCM satisfiability problem) and instead develop a novel two-step technique combining structural characterizations of well-formed SCMs with tailored linear programs of bounded size. This is a genuine methodological contribution that could be reused in other settings combining discrete structure with continuous probability parameters.

The results are comprehensive and tight: for both the SAT^lin_prob (parameterized by treewidth+domain size) and SAT^lin_counterfact (parameterized by n+domain size) settings, the authors provide matching FPT/XP algorithms and matching lower bounds (NP-hardness/W[1]-hardness) that pin down exactly where tractability starts and stops across the full 3x3 expressivity matrix, including the poly fragment (via ∃R-hardness) and the base fragment restricted to very simple structural instances (bounded degree, disjoint paths, edgeless graphs).
Proofs are detailed, mostly self-contained, and illustrated with a worked example (Example 6) that makes the fairly abstract LP construction concrete and easy to follow.

The discussion of the marginalization extension (bounded-depth summation operator) and its limits (NEXP-completeness precluding EXPTIME-based tractability) reflects careful attention to the boundaries of the results and honest treatment of what is and is not achieved.

Related work is thorough, correctly situating the paper relative to prior classical complexity results (Fagin-Halpern-Megiddo, Mossé-Ibeling-Icard, van der Zander et al., Dörfler et al.) and to parameterized-complexity work on Bayesian network structure learning and other treewidth applications in AI.
weaknesses: The paper is purely theoretical with no empirical evaluation or discussion of practical implementation; while this may be appropriate for a complexity-theory contribution, the ICML venue typically expects some discussion of practical relevance, e.g., how large treewidth/domain size instances arising in real causal-inference problems tend to be, or a proof-of-concept implementation, which is entirely absent.

The main tractability results, while theoretically satisfying, come with runtimes that are very large in practice (e.g., d^{f(tw)} or n! · d^{O(n^2)} for the counterfactual case), and no attempt is made to give concrete bounds on f(tw) or discuss whether the algorithms could be practically implementable even for small parameter values; the significance of the results for actual causal-inference practitioners is therefore unclear.

The scope of positive results is fairly narrow: FPT/XP tractability is only shown for the 'lin' fragment without the full marginalization/summation operator (only bounded nesting depth is handled), and the treewidth-based result is restricted to the prob layer (no interventions), while the counterfactual result abandons treewidth entirely in favor of parameterizing by the raw number of variables n, which is a much less refined and less practically useful parameter (many real causal graphs have small treewidth but large n).

Some hardness results rely on somewhat contrived structural restrictions (e.g., Theorem 1's arbSAT construction, Theorem 9's vertex-disjoint paths of length 2) whose direct relevance to naturally occurring causal reasoning instances is not discussed; it would strengthen the paper to relate these restrictions to realistic causal modeling scenarios.

The presentation, while rigorous, is extremely dense and notation-heavy (e.g., the definitions of E_prop, E_int, T_base/lin/poly, the LP constructions in Theorem 5 and Lemma 10/Theorem 11) which may limit accessibility to a broader ICML audience not already steeped in the PCH complexity literature; a higher-level intuition section or diagram summarizing the LP construction technique would improve readability.

The paper does not discuss whether the identified FPT results could lead to any approximate or heuristic methods for the intractable fragments (poly, or full marginalization), leaving open how the theoretical gateways to tractability might translate into partial practical progress on the harder but more expressive fragments that are arguably of most interest in applications.

strengths: The paper is technically rigorous: it provides a comprehensive, tightly matched set of upper and lower bounds covering the parameterized complexity landscape of SAT in several fragments of Pearl's Causal Hierarchy (probabilistic, causal, counterfactual; base/linear/polynomial breadth), with hardness results (NP-, W[1]-, and ∃R-hardness) that precisely delimit the reach of the positive algorithmic results.

The core technical idea—departing from the standard dynamic-programming paradigm for treewidth and instead constructing a 'fixed-parameter sized' linear program by exploiting a well-structured characterization of satisfying SCMs—is a genuinely novel proof technique for treewidth-parameterized tractability that could plausibly transfer to other problems combining discrete structure with continuous/probabilistic elements.
The writing is generally careful and the results are clearly summarized (contributions box, Figure 1 mind-map), and a worked example (Example 6) helps make the abstract LP construction concrete.

The paper is honest about the limits of its own results, explicitly noting where tractability cannot be lifted (polynomial fragments, marginalization with unbounded summation depth) and grounding these claims in matching hardness reductions rather than merely asserting difficulty.
weaknesses: The submission is purely a complexity-theoretic/algorithmic-existence paper: there is no implementation, no empirical evaluation, and no discussion of whether real causal-inference problem instances actually exhibit small primal treewidth or small numbers of observed variables, making the practical significance of the 'gateways to tractability' largely speculative for an ICML audience.

The XP algorithm for the counterfactual fragment (Theorem 11) relies on brute-force enumeration over all n! variable orderings combined with an LP of size roughly d^{n^2}; while this technically establishes XP/FPT membership, it is an extremely weak form of tractability that is unlikely to be usable in practice, and the paper does not discuss whether tighter algorithms are plausible or provide any complexity-theoretic intuition for why n! is unavoidable beyond the stated lower bounds.

Several of the 'novel' components are relatively close in spirit to well-known junction-tree/message-passing constructions from the probabilistic graphical models literature (propagating consistent local distributions along a tree decomposition via an optimization program); the paper could more explicitly contrast its LP-based approach with junction-tree algorithms to substantiate the claimed novelty.

The significance of the results for the broader ICML audience is unclear: the paper is narrowly targeted at a specific complexity-theoretic open question in the PCH literature, with essentially no discussion of downstream implications for causal discovery, causal effect estimation, or any learning task that ICML attendees would typically care about.

The presentation is dense and notation-heavy (e.g., the syntax/semantics section, nice tree decomposition definitions, ETR reductions), which, combined with the absence of any intuitive high-level exposition of why treewidth-based DP fails for this problem before diving into the LP construction, may limit accessibility even for readers versed in parameterized complexity but not causal inference formalism (or vice versa).

strengths: The paper provides the first systematic parameterized-complexity analysis of Satisfiability across the full expressivity matrix (depth × breadth) of Pearl's Causal Hierarchy, delivering a comprehensive and largely tight picture (matching FPT/XP algorithms with hardness lower bounds) rather than isolated positive results.

Technically novel proof technique: rather than the standard dynamic-programming approach used for essentially all prior treewidth-based tractability results (e.g., for SAT and CSP), the authors show that YES-instances admit 'well-structured' SCMs whose hidden-variable structure can be inferred from the tree decomposition in advance, reducing satisfiability to solving a fixed-parameter-sized linear program. This is a genuinely new algorithmic idea that could be of independent interest beyond this specific problem.

The lower bounds are carefully crafted to match the upper bounds under the exact same restricted settings (e.g., domain size 2, bounded degree, or specific graph shapes), which convincingly delineates the tractability frontier rather than leaving gaps.

The presentation is generally very clear for a dense technical topic: the paper is well organized, includes a helpful mind-map figure summarizing all eight numbered results, and includes a fully worked-out example (Example 6) that makes the abstract LP construction concrete.

The related work section is thorough, correctly situating the contribution relative to prior classical-complexity results (Fagin et al., Mossé et al., van der Zander et al., Dörfler et al.) and to other treewidth-based algorithmic work in AI, and explicitly explains why this work's technique differs.

The discussion of the marginalization extension is honest and precise, explaining exactly why the results cannot be lifted to unbounded summation depth (matching known NEXP/EXPTIME separations) while still noting the partial applicability to bounded nesting depth.
weaknesses: The paper is purely theoretical with no empirical or illustrative validation of practical significance—there is no discussion of whether treewidth or number-of-variables parameters are actually small in realistic causal models arising in practice, which would strengthen the case that these are true 'gateways to tractability' rather than only theoretically interesting classes.

Several of the positive results are only XP (not FPT) when parameterized by treewidth or n alone, and become FPT only when combined with the domain size d; since domain size is often unbounded or large in real applications (e.g., continuous or high-cardinality variables), the practical reach of the FPT results is limited, and this caveat could be discussed more critically in the concluding remarks rather than simply being stated as a hardness result.

The restriction of tractability to the 'lin' fragment (linear combinations of probability terms) leaves the 'poly' fragment intractable across the board, and while this is consistent with known ETR-hardness, the paper could better discuss the practical loss of expressivity this entails for real causal-reasoning tasks that may require nonlinear/product terms (e.g., certain identification queries).

Fit with the ICML audience is a mild concern: the paper is essentially a parameterized-complexity theory contribution with dense formalism (grammars, tree decompositions, ETR reductions) and might be more naturally at home in a theoretical computer science venue; a broader discussion connecting the results back to concrete ML/causal-inference use cases would help ICML readers appreciate the significance.

The treatment of limitations is fairly minimal—the 'Concluding Remarks' section is short and mostly poses open questions (marginalization, further applications of the LP technique) rather than critically reflecting on the scope and practical limitations of the current results (e.g., runtime blow-up d^{tw} or d^{n} even in the tractable regimes, which may still be prohibitive for moderate parameter values).

strengths: The paper opens up an entirely new research direction for the well-studied Satisfiability problem in Pearl's Causal Hierarchy by applying parameterized complexity, a lens that had not previously been used in this area despite the near-universal NP-/∃R-hardness of the classical problem.

The technical contribution is genuinely novel: the authors explicitly depart from the standard dynamic-programming paradigm used for essentially every prior treewidth-parameterized algorithm (e.g., for SAT and CSP) and instead develop a two-step approach that (i) shows every YES-instance admits a 'well-structured' SCM whose hidden-variable structure mirrors the tree decomposition, and (ii) encodes the existence of a valid probability distribution as a fixed-parameter-sized linear program. This LP-based treewidth technique appears to be a new algorithmic tool that could have broader applicability, as the authors themselves note.

The results form a comprehensive and essentially tight map of the parameterized landscape (Figure 1): FPT/XP positive results for SATlin_prob (w.r.t. tw+d) and SATlin_counterfact (w.r.t. n+d) are complemented by matching hardness results (W[1]-hardness, no-XP/no-FPT results, and ∃R-hardness for poly fragments) that pin down the boundaries of tractability, giving the reader a essentially complete picture rather than isolated positive or negative results.

The paper is technically careful: definitions (syntax/semantics of PCH fragments, primal treewidth, ETR) are precisely stated, an illustrative worked example (Example 6) is provided to make the LP construction concrete, and the proofs (e.g., Theorem 5, Lemma 10, Theorem 11) are detailed and appear internally consistent.

The related work section is thorough and clearly situates the contribution relative to prior classical-complexity results (Fagin et al., Mossé et al., van der Zander et al., Dörfler et al.) as well as parameterized-complexity work on adjacent problems (Bayesian network structure learning, causal discovery), and the paper explicitly discusses how its results interact with marginalization operators from very recent related work.
weaknesses: The paper is purely theoretical with no empirical component whatsoever; while this may be appropriate for a complexity-theoretic contribution, at a venue like ICML the practical implications of the results (e.g., whether the FPT/XP algorithms could ever be implemented or are useful in practice) are not discussed, and the extremely high parameter dependence of some algorithms (e.g., d^{d^n} in Theorem 11) suggests very limited practical applicability even on generously small instances.

The significance of the contribution to the broader ICML audience is somewhat narrow: the paper targets a specialized theoretical question (parameterized complexity of a decision problem in a specific causal-reasoning formalism) that is likely to be of primary interest to a small community working on causal-hierarchy complexity theory rather than to ML practitioners or even most causal-inference researchers.

The writing, while precise, is dense and heavily notation-laden throughout (Sections 2–5), which may limit accessibility; a running example or more intuition-building discussion connecting the technical machinery (e.g., why 'well-structured' SCMs suffice, or the intuition behind the LP constraints) to reader-friendly reasoning would strengthen presentation.

The open question left for future work (XP-algorithm for SATlin_counterfact parameterized by n alone) indicates the picture, while largely complete, is not fully closed, and the treatment of the marginalization extension is only briefly sketched (a few sentences) rather than being a fully worked-out formal result.

There is limited discussion of how tight the parameter choices (primal treewidth, number of variables, domain size) are in practice for real causal models arising in applications; a brief discussion of realistic magnitudes of these parameters in applied causal-inference settings would help calibrate the practical relevance of the tractability results.

strengths: The paper tackles an original and well-motivated question: whether parameterized complexity can offer gateways to tractability for the notoriously intractable Satisfiability problem in Pearl's Causal Hierarchy, a question that had not previously been studied from this angle.

The technical contribution is non-trivial: the authors depart from the standard dynamic-programming paradigm typically used for treewidth-parameterized algorithms and instead develop a structural characterization of 'well-structured' SCMs combined with a carefully constructed linear program, which is a genuinely novel algorithmic technique that could be of independent interest.

The complexity landscape mapped out is comprehensive and essentially tight: the paper provides matching FPT/XP algorithms and hardness results (NP-hardness, W[1]-hardness, ∃R-hardness) across multiple parameterizations (treewidth, domain size, number of variables) and across the prob/causal/counterfactual fragments, summarized clearly in a mind-map figure.
The proofs are detailed and mostly self-contained, with a worked example (Example 6) that helps clarify the rather involved LP construction underlying the main tractability result.

The related work section carefully situates the contribution relative to prior complexity-theoretic studies of PCH satisfiability and parameterized approaches to other causal-reasoning problems such as Bayesian network structure learning.
weaknesses: Significance for the ICML audience is questionable: this is a pure complexity-theory paper with no experiments, implementation, or empirical demonstration connecting the theoretical tractability results to practical causal-inference workloads; it is unclear whether real-world causal reasoning instances ever exhibit the bounded treewidth and small domain/variable-count combinations required for the stated FPT results.

The achieved tractability results are quite narrow in practical reach: the FPT algorithm for SATlin_counterfact depends on n and d jointly in a doubly-exponential way (d^{d^n}), and the probabilistic-layer result requires both treewidth and domain size to be simultaneously small, substantially limiting the scope of instances for which the results yield feasible algorithms.

The paper's scope is restricted to the 'base' and 'lin' breadth fragments without marginalization (except for a brief remark); the practically important 'poly' fragment and the summation/marginalization-extended languages are shown to remain intractable or are left largely unaddressed, limiting the overall coverage of the expressivity matrix.

The manuscript appears to be formatted using a LIPIcs/Dagstuhl-style template rather than the ICML format, suggesting it may have been prepared primarily for a theory venue (e.g., ICALP/STACS/MFCS); this raises concerns about fit with the ICML venue and whether sufficient effort was made to frame the contribution for an ML audience.

There is little discussion motivating why the specific parameters chosen (primal treewidth, domain size, number of variables) are meaningful or realistic for causal models arising in machine learning applications, leaving the practical significance of the 'gateways to tractability' largely unsubstantiated beyond the theoretical results themselves.

The paper does not discuss limitations of the approach in much depth (e.g., scalability of the constructed LPs in practice, numerical precision concerns within an LP solver for probability constraints, or the gap between FPT/XP existence and feasibility for even moderately sized instances).

strengths: The paper opens a genuinely new research direction by applying parameterized complexity analysis to the Satisfiability problem for Pearl's Causal Hierarchy, a setting previously studied almost exclusively through classical complexity lenses (NP/∃R-hardness results).

The results are comprehensive and tight: for each positive tractability result (FPT/XP by treewidth, FPT by n+domain size for counterfactual fragments), matching hardness results are provided that pin down exactly which parameter combinations are needed, yielding a essentially complete picture summarized cleanly in Figure 1.

The technical approach is genuinely novel: rather than the standard dynamic-programming paradigm used in essentially all prior treewidth-based tractability results (including for SAT and CSP), the authors use a two-step technique—proving existence of a 'well-structured' SCM aligned with the tree decomposition, then encoding the existence of compatible probability distributions as a polynomial-size linear program. This departure is well-motivated and could plausibly be reused in other AI/ML settings combining discrete and continuous structure, as the authors note.

The exposition is careful and includes a fully worked-out example (Example 6) that helps ground the abstract LP construction from Theorem 5, improving reproducibility/understandability of a dense technical proof.

The hardness reductions are varied and well-chosen (k-Multicolored-Clique, a restricted ETR variant, and 3-SAT), giving confidence that the negative results are not artifacts of a single reduction style, and the paper explicitly notes how its restricted syntax (sets of inequalities vs. arbitrary Boolean combinations) is justified by an additional hardness result (Theorem 1) rather than simply assumed for convenience.

Related work is thorough and situates the contribution clearly against both the PCH satisfiability literature and parameterized-complexity work on Bayesian network structure learning and other AI applications of treewidth.
weaknesses: The paper is purely theoretical with no implementation or empirical demonstration of the algorithms; while this is understandable for a complexity-theoretic contribution, it leaves the practical usefulness of the proposed FPT/XP algorithms (e.g., for realistic causal models) entirely unvalidated, and the stated running times (e.g., d^{d^n} n! for Theorem 11) suggest severe practical limitations even within the 'tractable' regime.

The scope of true tractability is fairly narrow: positive results are confined to the 'lin' breadth fragment and (for causal/counterfactual depth) require simultaneously bounding both the number of variables and domain size, which are strong restrictions; the 'poly' fragment and larger instances remain intractable, somewhat tempering the stated goal of finding broad 'gateways to tractability'.

The marginalization extension (a practically important feature per cited related work) is only handled under an arbitrary-but-fixed bound on nesting depth of the summation operator, and the paper does not explore whether more refined parameterizations (e.g., treewidth together with nesting depth) could help, leaving this an open question rather than a resolved contribution.

An explicit open problem (XP-algorithm for SAT^lin_counterfact parameterized by n alone) is left unresolved, which is reasonable to flag but means the counterfactual-layer complexity landscape is not as fully closed as the probabilistic-layer one.

The fit with the ICML audience is somewhat unusual given the heavy complexity-theoretic/TCS style of the paper (dense theorem-proof structure, ETR/∃R machinery); the paper would benefit from more intuition-building or discussion connecting the parameters (treewidth, domain size, n) to realistic causal modeling scenarios to help readers assess significance for ML practice.
